(this whole thing is about CK2 player, using all modern knowledge, to hunt for bloodlines to merge into their dynasty, and to have a descent from every famous historical, mythical, cultural house/figure possible. calculating eugenic programms {like Bene Gesserit with their Kwisatz Haderach, but this line is only for comparison}. for a player, using in-game ledgers, it's easy to track bloodlines passing, and see if the person is really carrying a bloodline or not. player chose the most optimal location, setting nice borders in early stages, and now is playing tall. the majority of bloodlines are patrilineal, meaning that they can't be passed through female by normal marriage. matrilineal marriage can be done, allowing matrilineal transfer from both parents, useful when the last member of bloodline is female. marriages inside dynasty, that are meant to slowly merge all collected bloodlines into the rulling branch, happen only between distant members, avoiding incest)

Here are two versions for you.

**Option 1** is a direct correction of your text. I have fixed the punctuation, spelling, and grammar while keeping your original phrasing and structure as close as possible.

**Option 2** is the **Narrative** you requested. It takes your ideas and rewrites them into a story told from the perspective of the "World," describing this strange CK2/CK3 player-dynasty.

***

### Option 1: Direct Correction (Punctuation & Grammar Check)

**The World’s POV:**

We see a peculiar, rising dynasty arranging marriages all around the globe. Their members intermarry equally with currently prosperous families and with families that are fading into obscurity for one reason or another. They don't seek conquest; in a set of decisive actions (not only war), they carved out their own domain once and then saw no need to expand their Archduchy any further.

Instead, they send their people searching for knowledge: genealogy, myths, and legends found in paper, oral traditions, rumors, and beliefs. They usually resolve things diplomatically, and the only wars they participate in are defensive. They accept people seeking a better life, such as those from declining houses, those whose royal families were overthrown, or those not first in the line of succession who likely won't inherit anything (except claims they will never have the means to realize). However, they don't accept everyone—only those listed as famous or notable in modern history.

They offer money and give better promises. They might "buy" a marriage from an unwilling parent. They don't care about a person's position in the line of succession. They might even invite people seemingly not descended from any famous house—if their origins are long forgotten, if they are from a cadet branch of a cadet branch many times removed, or if their ancestor was a bastard of someone notable whose lineage was forcibly forgotten.

They marry into families with claims of descending from someone significant. Whether this descent is acquired by diligent research (by the target family, though the Archduchy does research too), masterfully fabricated (for when many believe a lie, it becomes the truth) through money or cunning, or achieved by an ancestor’s actual deeds, the Archduchy’s dynasty "senses" if these claims are important.

Unlike others, they treat their women not as spare coins or incubators, but with respect, giving them time to decide if they like the groom chosen for them (the dynasty is vast, so it's easy to eventually find a compatible partner). This dynasty also looks for men and women—young or adult—with good qualities and talents. Most marry common members of the family, and only the best are groomed, educated, and married into the ruling line.

They often accept the last members of other dynasties into their family. It's not rare for them to set up matrilineal marriages. They value their women, so it is understandable when, after marrying some scion, the kids have the mother's dynasty name. However, sometimes they also marry distant nephews to women of other families on the condition that at least one child carries the father's dynasty name, allowing other kids to continue the mother's lineage. It doesn't bother them much if children from these unions don't carry their dynasty name, as long as it makes the bloodline continue. Only the ruling line demands all kids carry their dynasty name.

In the end, even when making marriages with someone seemingly insignificant, they still look like the winners.

***

### Option 2: The Narrative (The Story)

**The World's Perspective**

The world watched the rise of the Archduchy with a mixture of fear and confusion. In the beginning, they carved their borders with decisive, terrifying speed, employing steel and coin with equal efficiency. But the moment their domain was established, the expansion stopped. Their armies garrisoned the walls, and silence fell upon the borders. They did not want land; they wanted something else.

They sent out scholars instead of soldiers. These agents combed the libraries of the world, obsessed with genealogy, myths, and oral traditions. They sought blood.

To the great courts of Europe and beyond, their marriage habits were baffling. The Archduchy courted the powerful, certainly, but they seemed equally fascinated by the dying. They sought out families fading into obscurity—deposed royalty, fourth sons with no inheritance, and poverty-stricken nobles clinging to ancient names. They offered gold and sanctuary to those whom the rest of the world had discarded. They would "buy" a marriage from an unwilling lord or offer a haven to a princess with a claim she could never enforce.

It was as if they possessed a second sight. They found value in people the world deemed worthless. They would marry a peasant who was secretly the bastard of a saint, or a courtier descended from a hero of legend. Whether a lineage was proven by dusty records or fabricated until the lie became truth, the Archduchy knew. They could sense the greatness in the blood, collecting historical and mythical descendants with the precision of a collector pinning butterflies to a board.

Their domestic affairs were equally strange. They treated their daughters with unusual respect, refusing to use them as mere bargaining chips. Matrilineal marriages were common; they were fiercely protective of their own name, yet willing to help dying houses survive through complex contracts. They would marry a nephew to a foreign queen, asking only that one child carry the Archduchy's name while the rest continued the mother's line. They acted as preservationists, saving the bloodlines of others as long as a drop of it eventually flowed back into their own reservoir.

They hunted for talent as voraciously as they hunted for royalty. Strong men, genius women, and beautiful commoners were swept up into the fold. These talented souls were married into the cadet branches, a slow and deliberate process of refining the blood, breeding out weakness until the very best could be folded into the ruling line.

To the casual observer, the Archduchy appeared to be diluting its nobility with bastards, exiles, and nobodies. But as the generations passed, the world began to realize the truth. While other great houses inbred into madness or died out in petty wars, the Archduchy grew stronger, smarter, and more vibrant. They had merged the history of the world into a single family tree. Even when they made a match that seemed insignificant, they always, invariably, emerged as the winners.
